You found a Bitcoin backup. Take your time.

Nothing here is urgent. Bitcoin does not expire, and nobody can take it while the backup stays private. Go slowly, one step at a time, and do not let anyone rush you. This page works offline and sends nothing anywhere.

  1. Keep it private. Do not type the words into a website, an app or a phone, and do not photograph them. Never give them to anyone: no real company, exchange, lawyer or support person ever needs them. Anyone who asks for them, or offers to recover the money for a fee, is a thief.
  2. What do you have?
    • 12 or 24 words (sometimes 15, 18 or 21): a seed phrase, also called a recovery phrase. The words are the wallet.
    • Words plus another word or sentence, called a passphrase or 25th word: both are needed, exactly as written (capital letters and spaces count).
    • A metal plate or cards with words or their first letters: the same words, stamped so they survive fire and water.
    • 12 words from an Electrum wallet made before version 2.0: an old Electrum seed. Some of its words are not on the usual list. VERIFY recognizes it and shows its addresses; it opens in Electrum.
    • A small device (Trezor, Ledger, Coldcard, BitBox, Jade and others): a hardware wallet. It needs its PIN; the words written for it open the wallet without the device.
    • Several sets of words, or a note like “2 of 3” or “multisig”: a multisig wallet. It needs more than one set of words plus the wallet’s setup file (a descriptor). Set up a multisig wallet, in EXTRA TOOLS, explains it.
    • A long code starting with xpub, ypub or zpub: a watch-only key. It shows the balance but cannot spend.
    • A code starting with bc1, 1 or 3: an address. It shows where money was received; it cannot spend.
    • A code that starts with 5, K or L, or with xprv: a private key, as on an old paper wallet. Treat it like the words.
    • A VOIDFORGE BACKUP PLAN sheet: it says where the copies are, what wallet app was used and who can help. It holds no words.
  3. Check that the words are complete and right. VERIFY says whether they make a valid backup, and its fingerprint is the wallet’s name tag. If a word is missing, wrong or hard to read, Reforge (in EXTRA TOOLS) can often find it: for a burned or rusted word, type the letters you can read with ? for each one you cannot.
  4. Find the wallet. If the right words open an empty wallet, the app may be looking in the wrong place. If you know one address the wallet used (from old emails, statements or exchange withdrawals), the Wallet Detective finds which app made it and how to open it.
  5. See the balance without risk. After VERIFY, Open this wallet lists the wallet’s addresses, 10 at a time. Compare them with old statements or exchange withdrawals, or look one up in a block explorer on another device: it shows the balance, and the words never touch an online device.
  6. Move the money only when you are ready (and, for an inheritance, after legal advice). Install a well-known wallet app from its own website, or use a hardware wallet, restore the words there, send a small test amount first, and keep the words private until everything is moved.
Scam warnings.
  • Nobody genuine will ever ask for the words, the passphrase or a photo of them.
  • “Recovery services” and “support agents” who contact you first are thieves, however official they look.
  • Fake wallet apps copy real names. Install apps only from the maker’s own website, never from a link someone sent you.
  • Never type the words into a website, even one that says it checks them.
  • Ask people you already trust for help, not people who found you. An estate lawyer needs to know the wallet exists, never the words.

  2. Roll
  3. Forge
  4. Passphrase
  5. Check

MAKE A SEED

Pick 12 or 24 words, enter your dice rolls or coin flips, then press FORGE SEED and write the words on paper.

Step 1 of 5

Choose how your seed is made

Your wallet starts as a very large random number. Real dice (or a coin) are how you create it yourself, instead of trusting a computer to pick it. First choose the length: 12 words is strong enough for almost everyone and needs about 50 dice rolls. 24 words is the longest option and needs about 99 rolls. (15, 18 and 21 words are there too, for wallets that take them.) Then choose dice (easier for most people) or coin (many more flips). If you have physical word tiles, use the Word draw box instead. Making real keys? First read “Before you make real keys” (the Read before real keys link near the top of the page).

Roll your dice

Roll a real die, then tap the number it shows. Do not make numbers up: people are bad at being random, and the whole point is that nobody could guess your rolls. You need at least 50 rolls; more are fine, and every one counts. The bar fills as you go, and NEXT unlocks when you have enough. The gray words below change with every roll, so you can see how one roll changes every word. Make sure nobody can see your screen.

Forge the seed and write it down

Press FORGE SEED. Your rolls are scrambled together into your seed words. (A passphrase, if you want one, comes next, after you can see the words.) Write the words on paper, in order, with a pen. Never take a photo, type them into a connected device, or store them in a cloud. Anyone who has these words has your money. NEXT unlocks once the words are shown.

Optional: add a passphrase

A passphrase is an extra secret that makes a different wallet from the same words. It protects you if someone finds your paper, but if you lose it the funds are gone for good. If you are not sure, skip this step. If you want one, type it twice in the Passphrase box under your words. The page then shows the fingerprint without the passphrase and with it, so you can see they are different wallets. Write the passphrase down separately from the words.

Check it and make a backup

Last step, and the most important. Compare the fingerprint and the first ten receive and ten change addresses in a second wallet app, make a paper backup if you like (SeedQR or the printed sheet), then press START DRILL in the Restore drill below: it hides the words on screen and has you type them back from your paper. (The CHECK A BACKUP tab can also check words you already have.) Start with a small amount first.

Word draw: made your words with physical tiles?SECRETType words drawn from word tiles (such as SeedSigner’s SeedPills) or picked with dice (such as BitBox02’s diceware table), plus a few coin flips.
How Word draw works

Word tiles let you pick the words by hand: mix them in a bag, draw one without looking, flip it to choose a face, write the word down and put the tile back before the next draw. Each word is 11 random bits. A 12-word seed needs 11 drawn words and 7 coin flips; a 24-word seed needs 23 words and 3 flips (15 words: 14 and 6; 18 words: 17 and 5; 21 words: 20 and 4). The flips are needed because part of the last word is a checksum. Type your words (the first four letters of each are enough) and your flips; VOIDFORGE finishes the last word the standard BIP39 way, with no hashing, so any BIP39 wallet reads the result. Repeated words are fine, because every draw goes back in the bag. It never fills in the flips for you. Typed words are secret: use it only where nobody can see your screen.

Using dice instead of tiles?
Type a word number (1–2048), or a D8 roll followed by two 16-sided dice (0–F), written with a space between them, such as 3 A 7 (a plain number with no spaces is a word number). The word number is (D8 − 1) × 256 + the two hex digits + 1. For the final word of a 24-word seed, a last D8 roll gives 3 bits: write it as flips (1 = 000, 2 = 001 ... 8 = 111).
Using BitBox02’s diceware table?
BitBox02 diceware makes a 24-word seed. For each of the first 23 words, roll four dice, then a fifth, re-rolling any 5 or 6 so every die shows 1 to 4, and flip a coin. Type them like 2143 2 T (the four dice, the fifth die, H or T) and press ADD WORD or Enter: you get the same word as BitBox’s printed table. For the last word, BitBox shows 8 choices and you flip 3 coins (HHH picks the first, TTT the eighth). Type those 3 flips in the flips box below with T as 1 and H as 0 (HHT is 001), and the page makes the same 24th word BitBox would.
The passphrase (if any) is added after the words are made, in the box under them. Coin: pick which side is 1 and keep it the same for every flip (for BitBox02’s last word, T is 1 and H is 0).
Cards and hexSECRETMake a seed from a shuffled deck of playing cards, or from hex digits (a 16-sided die).
How cards work

Use a full deck of 52 cards with the jokers taken out. Shuffle it well (at least seven riffle shuffles), lay the cards out face up and type them in order, such as AS 10H QD 2C: the rank (A, 2 to 10, J, Q, K) and then the suit (C, D, H or S; ♠ ♥ ♦ ♣ work too). The Card method menu above decides how the cards become the seed. Both match Ian Coleman’s BIP39 tool, so you can check the words there (tick Use Entropy and type the cards with T for a 10, such as AS TH QD 2C).

Ian Coleman, hashed (every card counts), the default: VOIDFORGE writes the cards as A♠ 2♣ T♦ and so on and hashes that text with SHA-256. In his tool, set Mnemonic Length to the same number of words (not Use Raw Entropy). EntropyLab’s Coleman symbols option makes the same words. A 12-word seed needs 25 cards, 15 words 31, 18 words 39 and 21 words 50; a 24-word seed needs the whole deck and then 6 more from a new shuffle.

Ian Coleman, raw entropy: no hashing. Each card is turned into 5, 4 or 2 bits by his table, and the words are made from the last whole blocks of 32 bits (3 words per block); the first bits that do not fill a block are dropped. In his tool, leave Mnemonic Length on Use Raw Entropy (3 words per 32 bits), his first choice. The number of words follows from the cards, so deal until VOIDFORGE says enough. His tool counts each card as if it were put back in the deck; cards dealt from one deck hold less (his own notes: a full deck gives 225 bits, not 232), so VOIDFORGE shows the strength as “at most”. A whole deck makes 21 words.

Or hex: a 16-sided die, or checking another tool

Type exactly 32 hex digits (0 to 9 and a to f) for 12 words, 40 for 15 words, 48 for 18 words, 56 for 21 words or 64 for 24 words. They are used directly as the seed’s randomness, with no hashing, as in Ian Coleman’s tool with Hexadecimal and raw entropy chosen. For a real seed, roll a 16-sided die yourself (one digit per roll). Never use hex that a website or a program made for you.

The passphrase (if any) is added after the words are made, in the box under them.
The Damascus methodSECRETMake a seed by hand from dice and playing cards, folded together and checked at every step.
The Damascus method, created by Random, 10 November 2026

Make a seed by hand from dice and playing cards. The five steps follow the printed sheets: each says what to write on paper and what this page does with it. About 30 minutes on paper once you know the steps; allow longer the first time.

On this page you enter only the dice (step 1) and the cards (step 2), then press FORGE SEED. The page does the Forge, the words and the last word for you, as the other MAKE A SEED tabs do. Steps 3 to 5 are the paper path: do them on the Forge sheet, and type what you wrote here only if you want each one checked. Using only the page means trusting its math, as with the other methods; doing steps 3 to 5 on paper is how you check every bit yourself, without trusting any device.

Guided practice

Step 1 of 5: The Hammer (dice)

On paper: the Hammer sheet (H1 to H3)

  1. Throw both dice. Read the left die first.
  2. Write both numbers in the next pair box.
  3. Rolled 1-1, 2-2, 3-3 or 4-4? Cross the pair box out and throw both dice again.
  4. Look up the pair in the mirror table on the Hammer sheet (a pair and its mirror, like 2-5 and 5-2, share the first 4 bits): the row is the left die, the column is the right die. It gives you 5 bits (like 01101).
  5. Write the 5 bits into the next shaded run of the grid (a run is the stretch of boxes for one pair or one group of cards, shaded and white in turn).
  6. Repeat until the grid is full (26 good pairs). The last pair uses only 3 bits.
  7. Dice check: in the first 26 pair boxes, including crossed-out boxes: 52 numbers, count how often each face came up, and count the repeats (a number the same as the number just before it, reading every number in order: left, right, then the next box). FAIL if any count is 18 or more, or 1 or fewer, or repeats are 2 or fewer. On a FAIL, use other dice and start a new Hammer sheet.
  8. A hallmark is a check bit: whether a row or a column holds an odd or an even number of 1s (its parity).
  9. Row hallmark R: count the 1s in the row and write the result in the R box at the end of the row: odd: 1 3 5 7 9 11 → 1 · even: 0 2 4 6 8 10 → 0.
  10. Column hallmark M: count the 1s in the column and write the result in the M box under it, the same way.

On this page

Tap the left die, then the right die: two taps for each pair, crossed-out pairs too. Or type the pairs, two numbers each, such as 14 15 26.

Grid H
Optional: type your hallmarks as you count them; each row and column is checked as you type it.

What you should have now: 26 good pairs in the pair boxes, grid H full (rows 1 to 11 with 11 bits, row 12 with 7), and PASS in the dice check.

Step 2 of 5: The Anvil (cards)

On paper: the Anvil sheet (A1 to A4)

  1. Shuffle well: spread the cards face down and swirl them for 30 seconds, riffle shuffle 12 times, then cut.
  2. Deal 8 cards face up in a row.
  3. Play the 7 matches shown on the sheet: 1 against 2, 3 against 4, 5 against 6, 7 against 8, then the two winners on the left, then the two winners on the right, then the final. In each match write 1 if the right card is higher, 0 if the left card is higher. A group of 8 cards (an octet) gives 7 bits for its run of grid A; a group of 4 (a quad) gives 3.
  4. Deal the next 8 cards and play again: 6 groups of 8 in all. Then deal 4 cards: 1 against 2, 3 against 4, then the two winners.
  5. Do it 3 times in all: shuffle the same deck again each time. The last deck is shorter: on deck 3, deal 5 groups of 8, then 4 cards, and stop.
  6. Card check, while you deal: count the neighbors: two cards dealt one after the other in the same group, with the same suit and ranks next to each other (like 7♥ 8♥). Ace and King are not neighbors, and two cards in different groups never count. After each deck, count its 1s. FAIL a deck if its 1s are 11 or fewer, or 34 or more (full 45-bit decks only), or its neighbors are 6 or more. On a FAIL, shuffle again and redo that deck.
  7. Hallmarks R and M, the same way as on the Hammer sheet.

On this page

Tap each card as you deal it. The page deals them in groups as the sheet does and shows the bits each group gives. A card already dealt from this deck shows its back. Or type the card record, one deck a line, such as 9D 3S AC 10H.

Grid A

What you should have now: grid A full (128 bits, row 12 with 7), the card record if you keep one, and PASS for each deck.

Step 3 of 5: The Forge (XOR)

On paper. On this page it is optional: the page folds the grids itself once the dice and cards are in; type your hallmarks to have your own folding checked.

On paper: the Forge sheet (F1, F2)

0 0 → 0
1 1 → 0
0 1 → 1
1 0 → 1
  1. Lay the Hammer and Anvil sheets side by side.
  2. Work one row at a time: finger on the same row on both sheets.
  3. For every box (this is XOR): Same → 0. Different → 1. Write it in the same box on the Forge sheet.
  4. Hallmarks on the Forge sheet, R and M, the same way as on the Hammer sheet.
  5. The seal: for each R box and each M box, fold the Hammer hallmark with the Anvil hallmark (Same → 0. Different → 1.). The result must equal the Forge sheet’s hallmark.
  6. If one doesn’t match: the mistake is where that row and that column cross. Fix it before you go on.

On this page

The page shows grid F and its hallmarks below, worked out from your dice and cards. Optional: type your Forge sheet’s hallmarks as you finish each row, R(F), one bit a row, then M(F) under the columns, to check your own folding. Each row is checked as you type it, and a mistake is shown at its row and column.

Grid F

What you should have now: grid F full, its R and M boxes filled, and the seal agreeing in every box.

Step 4 of 5: The words

On paper. On this page it is optional: the page finds the words itself once the dice and cards are in; type the words you wrote to have each one checked.

On paper: the Forge sheet and the word table (F3, F4)

  1. Split each Forge row into 3 + 4 + 4 bits: block, row, column. Block: which of the word table’s 8 blocks; row and column: where the word sits in that block.
  2. Look up the word in the word table with those three parts and write it next to the row. No math needed.
  3. Check each word back: find it alphabetically in the table and make sure its bits match the row.

On this page

The page shows the words below, worked out from your dice and cards. Optional: type each word as you write it (the first four letters are enough) to have it checked against its row.

What you should have now: words 1 to 11 next to rows 1 to 11, each one checked back.

Step 5 of 5: The last word

On paper with a SeedSigner. On this page it is done for you once the dice and cards are in (below). Did it all on paper? The box under it works out the last word from your words and bits.

On paper: the Forge sheet, box 5 (F5)

  • Your Forge sheet’s last row gives the last word’s 7 bits (3 for 24 words). These are not new coin flips.
  • SeedSigner asks for them under ‘Coin flip entropy’. That is just its way of typing in 0s and 1s: enter each bit as Heads = 1, Tails = 0.
  • The device then calculates the checksum (4 bits for 12 words, 8 for 24) and shows the final word. VOIDFORGE must show the same word.
  1. On the SeedSigner: Tools > Calc 12th/24th word > 12 words > type words 1 to 11 > Build Final Word > Coin flip entropy > enter the 7 bits (Heads = 1, Tails = 0).
  2. Final Word Calc shows the last word. Press Next: the 12th Word screen shows the fingerprint.
  3. Compare the last word, the fingerprint and the first address with this page. They must match.

On this page

Did it all on paper? Work out the last word here

Type words 1 to 11 (1 to 23 for 24 words) and the 7 bits (3) of your Forge sheet’s last row. CALCULATE LAST WORD works like SeedSigner’s Calc 12th/24th word: the bits, then the checksum.

What you should have now: the 12th word, the same on both tools, and the same fingerprint and first address on both.

Print the sheets

Blank sheets are not secret. A filled-in Forge sheet is your seed.

The whole method on one page

How to make a Damascus seed. A Damascus seed is a normal 12-word Bitcoin seed that you make by hand from dice and playing cards, and check by hand as you go. Damascus steel is made by folding two different steels into one blade that is stronger than either. The Damascus method folds dice and cards into one seed.

Time: about 30 minutes once you know the steps; allow longer the first time. Practice first with a practice sheet (FILL IN A PRACTICE SHEET on the Damascus tab) or throwaway rolls. Never put money on a practice seed.

Field-tested: a hand-made Damascus seed checked on a real SeedSigner and in Sparrow (10 November 2026).

Each part below has the steps, one action per line, then What you should have now, then Why it works. The step labels on the printed sheets (H1, A2, F5 ...) are shown in brackets.

What you need
  • The printed sheets: Hammer (dice), Anvil (cards), Forge (the result), and the word table. Print them from VOIDFORGE: MAKE A SEED, the Damascus tab.
  • Two matching six-sided dice.
  • One deck of 52 playing cards.
  • A pencil.
  • An offline VOIDFORGE and a SeedSigner for the last word.

Work in a private room. Phones away.

Part 1: The Hammer (dice)
  1. Throw both dice. Read the left die first. (H1)
  2. Write both numbers in the next pair box.
  3. Rolled 1-1, 2-2, 3-3 or 4-4? Cross the pair box out and throw both dice again.
  4. Look up the pair in the mirror table on the Hammer sheet (a pair and its mirror, like 2-5 and 5-2, share the first 4 bits): the row is the left die, the column is the right die. It gives you 5 bits (like 01101).
  5. Write the 5 bits into the next shaded run of the grid (a run is the stretch of boxes for one pair or one group of cards, shaded and white in turn).
  6. Repeat until the grid is full (26 good pairs). The last pair uses only 3 bits.
  7. Dice check: in the first 26 pair boxes, including crossed-out boxes: 52 numbers, count how often each face came up, and count the repeats (a number the same as the number just before it, reading every number in order: left, right, then the next box). FAIL if any count is 18 or more, or 1 or fewer, or repeats are 2 or fewer. On a FAIL, use other dice and start a new Hammer sheet. (H2)

What you should have now: 26 good pairs in the pair boxes, grid H full (rows 1 to 11 with 11 bits, row 12 with 7), and PASS in the dice check.

Why it works
  • Bit: a 0 or a 1. Entropy: the randomness a seed is made from, 128 bits for 12 words.
  • Two dice have 36 results. The 4 doubles 1-1 to 4-4 are thrown again, so 32 are left: exactly the 32 codes of 5 bits, each as likely as the others with fair dice.
  • The fifth bit says which die was higher. It stays fair even with a biased die, because a die is as likely to be higher first as second.
  • The dice check catches badly broken dice, not small flaws. The cards cover the rest (Part 4).
Part 2: The Anvil (cards)
  1. Shuffle well: spread the cards face down and swirl them for 30 seconds, riffle shuffle 12 times, then cut. (A1)
  2. Deal 8 cards face up in a row. (A2)
  3. Play the 7 matches shown on the sheet: 1 against 2, 3 against 4, 5 against 6, 7 against 8, then the two winners on the left, then the two winners on the right, then the final.
    • The higher card wins and plays on.
    • In each match write 1 if the right card is higher, 0 if the left card is higher.
    • Ace is lowest, King is highest. For the same rank: clubs < diamonds < hearts < spades.
    • A group of 8 cards (an octet) gives 7 bits for its run of grid A; a group of 4 (a quad) gives 3.
  4. Deal the next 8 cards and play again: 6 groups of 8 in all.
  5. Then deal 4 cards: 1 against 2, 3 against 4, then the two winners.
  6. Do it 3 times in all: shuffle the same deck again (step 1) each time. The last deck is shorter: on deck 3, deal 5 groups of 8, then 4 cards, and stop.
  7. Card check, while you deal: count the neighbors: two cards dealt one after the other in the same group, with the same suit and ranks next to each other (like 7♥ 8♥). Ace and King are not neighbors, and two cards in different groups never count. After each deck, count its 1s. FAIL a deck if its 1s are 11 or fewer, or 34 or more (full 45-bit decks only), or its neighbors are 6 or more. On a FAIL, shuffle again and redo that deck. (A3)

What you should have now: grid A full (128 bits, row 12 with 7), the card record if you keep one, and PASS for each deck.

Why it works
  • Match bit: 1 if the right card is higher. In a well-shuffled deck, either card is equally likely to be the higher one, so each match is a fair bit.
  • Every card has its own place in the order (rank, then suit), so there are no ties.
  • The card check catches a lazy shuffle, not a small flaw. The dice cover the rest (Part 4).
Part 3: Hallmarks (parity) on each sheet

A hallmark is a check bit: whether a row or a column holds an odd or an even number of 1s (its parity). On the Hammer sheet and on the Anvil sheet: (H3, A4)

  • Row hallmark R: count the 1s in the row and write the result in the R box at the end of the row: odd: 1 3 5 7 9 11 → 1 · even: 0 2 4 6 8 10 → 0.
  • Column hallmark M: count the 1s in the column and write the result in the M box under it, the same way.

What you should have now: on both sheets, an R box filled on every row and an M box under every column.

Why it works
  • Parity: whether a count is odd or even. A hallmark is the parity of the 1s in its row or column.
  • One wrong box changes the parity of its row and of its column, so its hallmarks show where it is.
Part 4: The Forge (XOR)
  1. Lay the Hammer and Anvil sheets side by side. (F1)
  2. Work one row at a time: finger on the same row on both sheets.
  3. For every box (this is XOR): Same → 0. Different → 1. Write it in the same box on the Forge sheet.
  4. Hallmarks on the Forge sheet, R and M, the same way as in Part 3. (F2)
  5. The seal: for each R box and each M box, fold the Hammer hallmark with the Anvil hallmark (Same → 0. Different → 1.). The result must equal the Forge sheet’s hallmark.
  6. If one doesn’t match: the mistake is where that row and that column cross. Fix it before you go on.

What you should have now: grid F full, its R and M boxes filled, and the seal agreeing in every box.

Why it works
  • XOR (folding): two bits in, one bit out: 0 0 → 0, 1 1 → 0, 0 1 → 1, 1 0 → 1. Forge = Hammer XOR Anvil.
  • If either sheet is random, the Forge sheet is random too, even if the other sheet is bad or was made by someone you do not trust.
  • The parity of a folded row is the fold of the two parities. So the seal checks all your folding at once, without doing it again.
Part 5: The words
  1. Split each Forge row into 3 + 4 + 4 bits: block, row, column. Block: which of the word table’s 8 blocks; row and column: where the word sits in that block. (F3)
  2. Look up the word in the word table with those three parts and write it next to the row. No math needed.
  3. Check each word back: find it alphabetically in the table and make sure its bits match the row. (F4)

What you should have now: words 1 to 11 next to rows 1 to 11, each one checked back.

Why it works
  • The 11 bits of a row are the word’s place on the BIP39 list (2,048 words, from 0). The word table lays the list out by those bits, so no arithmetic is needed.
Part 6: The last word

Row 12 gives only 7 bits, because the last word also holds a checksum that needs a computer. (F5)

  • Your Forge sheet’s last row gives the last word’s 7 bits (3 for 24 words). These are not new coin flips.
  • SeedSigner asks for them under ‘Coin flip entropy’. That is just its way of typing in 0s and 1s: enter each bit as Heads = 1, Tails = 0.
  • The device then calculates the checksum (4 bits for 12 words, 8 for 24) and shows the final word. VOIDFORGE must show the same word.
  1. On the SeedSigner: Tools > Calc 12th/24th word > 12 words > type words 1 to 11 > Build Final Word > Coin flip entropy > enter the 7 bits (Heads = 1, Tails = 0).
  2. Final Word Calc shows the last word. Press Next: the 12th Word screen shows the fingerprint.
  3. In VOIDFORGE: MAKE A SEED > Damascus, step 5 (Last word). Type the same 11 words and the 7 bits, then press CALCULATE LAST WORD.
  4. Both must show the same last word, and it must be in the table row that the 7 bits point to.
  5. Compare the fingerprint on both. They must match.
  6. Compare the first address. On the SeedSigner: Load seed > Done > Address explorer > Native Segwit > Receive addresses, address 0. It must match VOIDFORGE’s first address.

What you should have now: the 12th word, the same on both tools, and the same fingerprint and first address on both.

Why it works
  • Checksum: the first 4 bits of SHA-256 of the 128 bits, added to the end so a wallet can tell a mistyped seed. Nobody can work out SHA-256 by hand, so two tools do it and must agree.
  • The 7 bits fix the table row, so a tool that gave a word outside that row would be wrong.
Part 7: Backup
  1. Copy the 12 words to your backup (paper or metal). (F6)
  2. Copy the hallmarks next to them (the row hallmarks and the column hallmarks). Later, anyone can recheck the words by hand with them.
  3. Keep the hallmarks only next to the words, because they reveal part of the seed.
  4. Destroy the sheets you do not keep. The Forge sheet is your seed.

What you should have now: the words and their hallmarks on your backup, and no other copy of the Forge sheet.

Why it works
  • The hallmarks reveal 22 bits of the seed: not enough to find it, but they make guessing easier. Next to the words they reveal nothing new.
24 words

The same steps, with 52 good dice pairs and 6 decks (on deck 6, the last: 4 groups of 8, then 4 cards). The last row has 3 bits, which pick one block of the word table; use 24 words on the SeedSigner. The dice check counts the first 52 pair boxes: 104 numbers, and FAIL if any count is 29 or more, or 6 or fewer, or repeats are 7 or fewer; the card check is the same. Allow about twice the time.

Doing it with a helper (optional)
  1. One person does the Hammer sheet, the other the Anvil sheet, in separate rooms.
  2. The card person writes down every card in the card record on the Anvil sheet.
  3. Each folds their sheet closed before seeing the other one. This matters: whoever sees the other sheet before finishing their own could steer the seed.
  4. Assay: later, each sheet can be checked by a different person (an assayer) without anyone learning the seed. In VOIDFORGE, choose "An assayer" under Who checks. Optional, for the assay: each sheet is also a Seed XOR part (step H4 on the Hammer sheet).
Check it all in VOIDFORGE (optional)

On the Damascus tab, the five steps (Hammer, Anvil, Forge, Words, Last word) follow these parts. Tap your dice and cards in as you go, or type them: VOIDFORGE checks each row, deck and word as you finish it, points to the box of any mistake, and works out the last word, fingerprint and first address. FORGE SEED then puts the seed into the page’s usual tools.

What the checks catch, and what they do not
  • The seal and hallmarks catch copying mistakes: every single slip, and nearly all bigger ones. They do not catch cheating.
  • The dice and card checks catch badly broken dice or a lazy shuffle, not small flaws. Having both dice and cards is what protects you: if either one is good, the seed is fully random.
  • Two tools agreeing on the last word, fingerprint and address shows the checksum is right.

The full method is in docs/damascus-method.md; the math and the tests are in docs/damascus-method-design.md.

Questions and fixes

Short answers for when something goes wrong. The steps are in docs/damascus-quick-guide.md.

I lost count while dealing
  1. Stop. Do not guess the bits you were not sure of.
  2. Cross out that deck’s runs in grid A.
  3. Gather the whole deck, shuffle it again (wash, 12 riffles, cut) and deal that deck again from its first group.
  4. With the card record, you can also redo the matches from the cards you wrote down.
A die rolled off the table

Throw that pair again. Only write a pair you saw land flat. A die that is tilted against something does not count either.

A bias box says FAIL
  • Dice: a fair pair of dice fails about 2 times in 100. Use other dice and start a new Hammer sheet. Never change the bits by hand.
  • Cards: a good shuffle fails about 6 decks in 1,000. Shuffle again and redo that deck.
  • The boxes only catch badly broken dice or a lazy shuffle. Small flaws pass. Using both dice and cards is what protects you.
The seal will not match
  1. Find the row whose hallmarks do not agree, and the column whose hallmarks do not agree.
  2. The mistake is in the box where that row and that column cross.
  3. Check that box three times: on the Hammer sheet, on the Anvil sheet, and the fold on the Forge sheet (same bits gives 0, different bits gives 1).
  4. If a row is off but no column is, the row hallmark itself may be miscounted. The same goes for a column.
  5. CHECK MY SHEETS in VOIDFORGE points to the box for you.
The two tools give different last words
  1. Check that both have the same 11 words (23 for 24 words), in the same order.
  2. Check the bits you typed for the last word: 7 bits for 12 words, 3 for 24. On the SeedSigner, Heads = 1 and Tails = 0.
  3. In VOIDFORGE, MAKE A SEED > Damascus, step 5 (Last word), type the same words and bits, in the same order.
  4. If they still differ, stop. Do not use the seed until you know why.
Are the last 7 bits coin flips?

No.

  • Your Forge sheet’s last row gives the last word’s 7 bits (3 for 24 words). These are not new coin flips.
  • SeedSigner asks for them under ‘Coin flip entropy’. That is just its way of typing in 0s and 1s: enter each bit as Heads = 1, Tails = 0.
  • The device then calculates the checksum (4 bits for 12 words, 8 for 24) and shows the final word. VOIDFORGE must show the same word.
How do I make 24 words?

The same steps, with 52 good dice pairs and 6 decks. Choose 24 words before you print the sheets. The last row of grid F has 3 bits, which pick one block of the word table; choose 24 words on the SeedSigner too.

Can I do it with a helper?

Yes.

  1. One person fills in the Hammer sheet and the other the Anvil sheet, in separate rooms.
  2. The card person writes down every card in the card record.
  3. Each folds their sheet closed before seeing the other one.

The order matters. Whoever fills in a sheet after seeing the other sheet can choose the seed, and every check still passes. Worked example 2 shows this.

Can I use only dice?

Yes: VOIDFORGE’s Dice tab does that. But then one bad die is not covered. With the Damascus method, the seed is fully random if either the dice or the shuffle is good.

Does my wallet take a Damascus seed?

Yes, if it takes standard 12- or 24-word BIP39 seeds. A Damascus seed is a normal BIP39 seed. Nothing about it shows how it was made.

What do the hallmarks reveal?

The row and column hallmarks reveal 22 bits of a 12-word seed (34 bits for 24 words; the two share one bit, the count of all the 1s). That is not enough to find the seed, but it makes guessing easier. Keep them only next to the words, never on their own. Anyone who has the words has the money anyway.

What is an assay?

Someone else (an assayer) checks one sheet only: the Hammer sheet, or the Anvil sheet with its card record. If the other sheet was made well and kept apart, one sheet shows nothing about the seed. In VOIDFORGE, choose "An assayer" under Who checks: it shows that sheet’s hallmarks and its own Seed XOR part, never the seed.

Worked examples (public: never put money on these)

Three worked examples to follow on paper or to load into CHECK MY SHEETS. They are public: never put money on them. Loading one turns on PRACTICE: FORGE SEED then shows the seed under YOUR SEED marked PRACTICE, with every step a real seed has.

Example 1. 12 words. Dice: the digits of pi (only 1 to 6, read in pairs). Cards: a published shuffle. Words: kick confirm home few coin pencil praise burst business fix credit sword. Fingerprint 70b5da37.

Example 2. 12 words. Dice: the digits of e. Cards: the card person saw the Hammer sheet first and placed the cards to steer the seed. It lands on a public test seed, and every check still passes: hallmarks catch mistakes, not cheating. This is why each sheet is folded closed before the other is seen. Words: legal winner thank year wave sausage worth useful legal winner thank yellow. Fingerprint b8688df1.

Example 3. 24 words. Dice: the digits of the square root of 2. Cards: a published shuffle, six decks. Words: candy play giraffe unable song nasty music stay nothing acquire cloud until logic key mango leopard true among genuine lucky family remain lesson artist. Fingerprint 116ab0ba.

DICE TEST ONLY: no seed is made from these rolls. Turn the test off in “Your rolls” below to make a seed.
Pick which side is 1 and which is 0 (the usual choice: heads = 1, tails = 0) and keep it the same for every flip. Only the 1/0 string is used, so any consistent choice is fine, but you cannot get the mapping back from the words. Write down the exact string or your mapping with your backup.
0 / 50 rolls
Your rolls: history and fairness chartSee what you rolled and whether the faces came up evenly, or test your dice without making a seed.
Roll together (two people or two dice)
Two or more people, or two or more dice, can make one seed together: each rolls with their own die, and all the rolls go into the roll box, in turn. Every roll is hashed together, but hashing only mixes the rolls; it cannot add randomness. So let each die roll the full count on its own (50 for 12 words, 99 for 24): for example 50 rolls with one die, then 50 with the other, 100 in all, and FORGE hashes every one. Then the words are random as long as one of the dice is fair and rolled honestly: a loaded die, or someone who picks numbers instead of rolling, cannot make the seed predictable. Using dice from two different shops protects you from one bad die. Everyone who sees all the rolls can make the seed again, so roll together only with people you would trust with the seed itself, and keep the rolls as secret as the words.
YOUR SEED
SECRET These words are your money. Write them on paper and never share them.
—
Passphrase and note (optional)A passphrase makes a different wallet from the same words. The note is only for you; it is not part of the seed.
About passphrases
A passphrase makes a different wallet from the same words. Write it down separately: without it the funds cannot be recovered. Some hardware wallets limit how long a passphrase can be or which characters it can use, so test a small amount on your device before you rely on it.
Make a passphrase from dice
Roll a die again, separately from the rolls for your seed, and these new rolls become a passphrase of BIP39 words. They are hashed with SHA-256, as for the seed, and each word takes the next 11 bits. Keep the passphrase apart from the seed words: anyone with both can spend, and the words alone open a different wallet. Choose 6 or 8 words: fewer could be searched by someone who has your seed words.

      Auto-clear: let the page wipe itselfOptional. Off unless you turn it on.
      
Off by default. When on, VOIDFORGE wipes the seed, rolls, passphrase and results without asking, so words are not left on the screen if you walk away. Write your words down first: a wipe cannot be undone. Nothing about this setting is saved; it is off again when the page reloads.

      

      
      

    

    
    

      Re-hide: cover secrets when you look awayOn. Nothing is wiped: tap SHOW to see them again.
      
While words, rolls, a passphrase or another secret are on the page, VOIDFORGE covers them again when you switch to another tab or app, when you click another window, when you print the page with the browser’s own Print, and after a while with no activity. Text is blurred; QR codes and other pictures are taken off the screen. Passphrase boxes go back to dots. VOIDFORGE’s own PRINT buttons still print what they say. The practice signer is covered while it holds a seed that is not public, a seed is being loaded or a passphrase is typed on it. Nothing about this setting is saved; it is back to 5 minutes when the page reloads.

            Words on other media
            
    
            
      Recheck a Damascus backupSECRETType the words and the hallmarks written next to them: VOIDFORGE says whether they match, or which word is most likely wrong.
      
            A Damascus backup keeps the row hallmark R of each word and the column hallmark M (and maybe the skew hallmark K) with the words. They catch any single wrong word except a wrong last word from the same table row (block, for 24 words): its last bits are not in the hallmarks, so only the checksum catches it, and RECHECK checks the checksum too. By hand: look up each word in the binary word table, write its 11 bits in a blank Forge grid (the last word: its first 7 bits, or 3 for 24 words), count the hallmarks again (an odd number of 1s gives 1) and compare.

What you type or tick here is as secret as the words: use an offline computer, and press CLEAR when you are done.             My wallet shows zero: Wallet DetectiveUSES THE WORDS ABOVE
            
      
            When the right words open an empty wallet, the app is often looking in a different place: another address type, account or path, a passphrase, or an Electrum seed. Type the words (and the passphrase, if any) in the boxes at the top of this tab, then one address you know this wallet received to (from an old message, invoice or exchange withdrawal). FIND MY WALLET tries the settings of well-known wallet apps until that address matches, then names the apps that use them and how to open it. It never looks up a balance. A search can take a minute or two (longer with a passphrase); STOP ends it. No address? LIST FIRST ADDRESSES shows the first address of each common setting, to look up on another device.
            
      
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
    
            
    
            
      
            Is this seed in my wallet file?USES THE WORDS ABOVE
            
      
            For a multisig wallet (or any wallet with a descriptor): paste its setup file, the output descriptor, the Coldcard multisig setup file or the BSMS record (or choose the file), with the seed words (and passphrase, if any) typed in the boxes above. VOIDFORGE checks every key in the file: is it made by this seed, with the fingerprint, path and key all matching? So you know which key of the wallet this backup is, before you rely on it. The file holds only public keys.
            
      
      
      
            
      
            
    
            
    
            
      
            Open an encrypted descriptor backup (BIP138)USES THE WORDS ABOVE
            
      
            A .bip138 file (made by Liana or by VOIDFORGE) holds a wallet’s descriptor, encrypted with the wallet’s own public keys. Choose the file or paste its text, then type the words of ONE of the wallet’s keys in the boxes at the top of this tab (with its passphrase, if it has one), or paste one of the wallet’s public keys (xpub) below: a public key opens it too. VOIDFORGE shows the descriptor, its checksum, the first 10 receive and 10 change addresses, and which key opened it.
            
      
      
      
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
    
            
    
            No words? Open a wallet file
            
    
            
      Open a signing device’s backupSECRETOpen an encrypted TAPSIGNER, Krux or Coldcard backup offline: which wallet it holds, and its seed.
      
            An encrypted backup a signing device wrote: a TAPSIGNER backup (.aes) with the key printed on the back of the card, a Krux encrypted seed (the encrypted QR’s text, or seeds.json) with its key, or a Coldcard backup (.7z) with its 12 backup words. VOIDFORGE opens it here, offline, and shows which wallet it holds (the fingerprint and first addresses). The backup holds the wallet’s private keys: open it only on your offline computer.
            
      
      
            
      
      
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
    
            
    
    
            
      Open an Electrum wallet fileSECRETRead an Electrum wallet file offline: what kind of wallet it is, its keys and first addresses, and its seed with the password.
      
            Electrum keeps each wallet in one file, in the wallets folder of its data folder: ~/.electrum on Linux and macOS, %APPDATA%\Electrum on Windows (the file is default_wallet unless you named it; testnet wallets are under testnet). Choose the file, drop it on this box or paste its text, and type the wallet password if it has one. VOIDFORGE only reads it: the file is never changed and nothing leaves the page. It reads files from Electrum 1.x to 4.8: wallets from an Electrum seed, a BIP39 seed or a master key, old seeds from before Electrum 2.0, imported addresses and private keys, hardware wallet and watch-only files, multisig and two-factor (2FA) wallets, with the keys encrypted with the password or the whole file encrypted. It cannot open a file encrypted with a hardware wallet, and it does not show Lightning channels.
            
      
      
            
      
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
    
            
    
    
            
      Read a Bitcoin Core wallet file (wallet.dat)SECRETChoose an old wallet.dat: see what it holds and, with its passphrase, its private keys.
      
            For a wallet.dat from Bitcoin Core (Bitcoin-Qt): an older legacy wallet (a Berkeley DB file) or a newer descriptor wallet (an SQLite file). VOIDFORGE reads it here, offline, and never changes it. It shows how the wallet was made, its keys, descriptors, address book labels and first addresses. If the wallet is encrypted, type its passphrase: VOIDFORGE checks it the way Bitcoin Core does and can then show the private keys. The file holds the private keys (encrypted or not): open it only on your offline computer, and use a copy, never your only one.
            
      
      
            Or drop the file on this box.
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
        
            What it holds
            
        
        
            
        
            
        
            
      
            
      
            
      
            
    
            
    
            Practice and plan
            
    
            
      Practice making a backupSECRETRehearse writing words on paper and checking them, with a public test seed or with your own words.
      
            Copying words by hand is where real backups go wrong. Write the words on paper, press HIDE, then type them back from the paper: the page checks the copy word by word. Rehearse with a public test seed (published test seeds from the BIP39 standard, for practice only: never put money on them), or check a real paper backup with your own words.
            
      
            
        
        
      
            
      
            
        
            Your own words open your wallet: do this only on your offline computer. Nothing is saved. Re-hide covers them; CLEAR, CLEAR ALL, auto-clear and END SESSION wipe them.
            
        
      
            
      
            
      
            
        
            PRACTICE ONLY. Never put money on this public test seed. Write the 12 words on paper, in order, with a pen. Then press HIDE.
            
        
            
        
              
        
      
              
      
              
        
              The words are hidden. Read your paper and type the words back, in order.
              
        
        
              
      
              
      
              
      
              Practice mode for the whole page
              
      
              Rehearse the whole job with worthless test coins. While it is on, every address on the page is on the test network (tb1..., 2..., m... or n...), the network menus stay on Testnet, and printed sheets with addresses or keys say TESTNET. A seed made while it is on is an ordinary seed: the test network only changes which addresses are shown, and seed backups print as usual. Turn it on or off when no multisig wallet is being made. While it is on, a PRACTICE MODE note sits under every network menu. OPEN A PRACTICE WALLET opens the words chosen above in CHECK A BACKUP, on the test network: the public test seed, to try receiving test coins with nothing at stake, or your own words, to see your own wallet’s test-network addresses (they are not your real addresses).
              
      
      
              
      
              
    
              
    
              
      Practice signer: works like SeedSignerSECRETThe same screens and buttons as a real SeedSigner, with step-by-step lessons, a practice transaction, and signing your own PSBTs and messages for real.
      
              A copy of SeedSigner 0.8.7 on the SeedSigner+ screen (320 x 240): the same screens, menus and buttons, and it does what the real device does.
              
      
              
        
              
          
          
          
          
          
          
              
          
          
          
        
              
      
              
      
              It runs inside this page, so it is as safe as the page itself: use it on an offline computer and write any seed on paper. Re-hide covers it while it holds a seed that is not public, and CLEAR ALL, auto-clear and END SESSION wipe it.
              
      
              
        
              Use the seed in VOIDFORGE
              
        
              FORGE SEED takes the seed loaded on the device, with its passphrase if one is applied, and shows it in MAKE A SEED like the other methods do: the words, fingerprint, addresses, SeedQR and watch-only wallet. A public seed (such as a lesson’s test seed) is marked PRACTICE; a seed made here from your own dice is not.
              
        
              
        
              
        
              Lessons
              
        
              Short lessons that walk you through the device, one press at a time. Each step moves on by itself when the device shows the right screen. They work with the seed loaded on the device, real or practice; with none loaded, they load the public test seed abandon ... about (anyone can make it, so never put coins on it). Their practice transactions spend made-up coins, so they can never be broadcast.
              
        
              
        
              
          
               · 
              
          
              
          
              
          
              
          
              
          
              
        
              
        
              Held up to the device’s camera: . 
              
        
              
        
              
        
              Practice transaction
              
        
              Makes a PSBT that spends made-up coins of the seed on the device and holds it up to the device’s camera. After you sign it, this page reads the signed PSBT from the device’s screen and checks every signature with its own code.
              
        
              
        
              Mainnet: these coins don’t exist; this PSBT can never be broadcast.
              
        
              
        
              
        
              
        
              Use it for real: your own PSBT, address, wallet or message
              
        
              A browser is not a hardware signer. This device signs for real, inside this page: a real SeedSigner keeps the seed off every computer, and this does not. With real coins, use it only on an offline computer you trust, check every address and amount on its screen against what you meant to send, and wipe the seed afterwards (CLEAR ALL).
              
        
              Paste a PSBT from your wallet (Sparrow, Electrum, Nunchuk, Specter, Bitcoin Core: base64, hex, or the parts of an animated UR or BBQr QR, one per line), an address to verify, a multisig wallet descriptor (sortedmulti), or a signmessage request; or choose a .psbt file, or scan a QR with this computer’s camera. HOLD UP TO THE DEVICE shows it to the device’s camera; then choose Scan on the device. The device reviews it and signs as SeedSigner does, and the signed PSBT comes back here too, byte for byte as in its QR code.
              
        
        
              
        
              
        
                
        
                Sign a message. Signed with the key of one of the seed’s single-key receive addresses, in the Bitcoin Signed Message format SeedSigner uses. Turn on Message signing on the device first (Settings > Advanced).
                
        
        
                
        
                
          
                
          
          
                
        
                
        
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      Backup plan and stress testNO WORDS, KEEP PRIVATEWhere your copies are, who can help, and what happens if something goes wrong. Printable.
      
                Fill in what is true for your wallet: places, people and how the passphrase is kept. Never type the words or the passphrase here. The stress test below updates as you type; nothing is saved. The printed plan says where your copies are, so keep it private and give it only to someone you trust.
                
      
                
        
        
        
        
      
                
      
                Copies of the words
                
      
                Copy 1
                
      
                Copy 2
                
      
                Copy 3
                
      
                If something happens to you
                
      
                
        
        
      
                
      
      
                Stress test: what happens if...
                
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  Inheritance documents
                  
      
                  Four more sheets for the people who would settle your estate: a letter for your lawyer or executor, recovery steps for your heir, the key details (public data only) and a sheet of trusted contacts. Like the plan, none of them holds the words or the passphrase, and they refuse to print if a box above looks like a secret. They use what you filled in above.
                  
      
                  
        
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  The key details sheet takes the fingerprint, address type, addresses and watch-only key from the wallet open in CHECK A BACKUP (type the words, then VERIFY), if its fingerprint is the one on this plan. Otherwise it prints blank lines to fill in by hand.
                  
      
                  
      
                  Tamper-evident bags
                  
      
                  A tamper-evident bag shows when it has been opened, and each bag has its own serial number. Seal each copy of the words in its own bag. Write down the serial (or photograph the sealed bag, never the words) and keep that record apart from the bag. At each check-up (the 5-minute routine on the printed plan), first check that the seal is intact and that the serial matches your record. A changed serial or a broken seal means: assume the backup was seen, and move the money to a new wallet. If you open a bag yourself to read the words, seal them in a new bag and write down its serial. PRINT BAG LOG prints a sheet for all of this.
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
  
                  
  
                  

  
                  
  
                  
    
                  EXTRA TOOLS
                  
    
                  Optional helpers. They only display; none of them can spend or sign.
                  
    
                  
      Reforge: recover a seed or find a passphraseSECRETMissing or wrong words, or a forgotten passphrase — search against what you already know.
      
                  Reforge searches for the words or passphrase you lost, checked against something you know is right: your wallet’s master fingerprint, one of its addresses, or its account xpub/zpub (all three are public, and a watch-only wallet shows them). It never guesses: it reports only what matched, and tells you plainly when nothing did. What you type here is secret; it is never saved or sent, and CLEAR wipes it.
                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  Type your words in order, with ? for each word you do not have. Reforge picks the search from what you type: with one or two ? it tries every word in those places; with all the words it tries every swap of two words and every single word replaced; with one word fewer (11, 14, 17, 20 or 23) it tries the missing word at every place. A word that is not on the BIP39 list counts as ?, and the first 4 letters of a word are enough. Damaged backup: inside a word, ? is one letter you cannot read and * any number of them, so ch?ir is chair and ab* is any word that starts with ab (4 readable letters are enough: c?ar fits charge and clarify), and a word written only as ??? counts as one you cannot read at all. Reforge says how many words fit each one and refuses more than 4,194,304 phrases. To list the words that could be last, type all but the last word, then ?. Two ? on a 12-word phrase can take a long time; an account xpub/zpub is by far the fastest thing to check against (a fingerprint or an address is several times slower), the page shows progress, and STOP ends the search.
                  
        
        
        
        
                  
          
          
          
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  For a wallet whose words you have but whose passphrase you do not remember exactly. Type your seed words, then your guesses or the pieces you remember, one per line, exactly as you might have typed them (spaces count). Reforge tries no passphrase, each line, and every two or three lines joined (with or without a space, in any order), each as typed, in lowercase, in UPPERCASE and Capitalised; tick one typo to also try each with a character missing, doubled, swapped with the next one, or in the other case. Each try takes the browser about a millisecond against an xpub/zpub and several times longer against a fingerprint or address, so the page counts the tries first and refuses more than 1,000,000.
                  
        
        
        
        
        
                  
          
          
          
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      Check your device’s diceTEST ONLYDoes your hardware wallet really make its words from your dice? Check it with throwaway rolls.
      
                  A hardware wallet that takes dice rolls should make its words from them alone. If its software ignored your rolls, the words would still look normal. So check it once: type the same throwaway rolls here and on the device, and the words must be the same. Then reset the device before making your real wallet, because test rolls and their words are not secret.
                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
      
                  0 / 50 rolls (exactly 50 for SeedSigner)
                  
      
                  
        
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
    
                  
      Practice your passphraseSECRETType it, then type it again from memory: see whether they match, and the fingerprint it gives.
      
                  A passphrase is used exactly as typed, and a wrong one opens an empty wallet without any warning. Rehearse it here: type it in the first box, then type it again from memory in the second (pasting is turned off there). Nothing is stored. The fingerprint below comes from the seed you choose with your passphrase. With the public test seed abandon ... about, load that test seed on a hardware wallet, type the passphrase on the device, and compare the fingerprint it shows. Keep that fingerprint private: with the public test seed, anyone who sees it can check guesses of your passphrase. With your own seed (typed here, or the one made on this page) it is your passphrase wallet’s real fingerprint, to compare with your device.
                  
      
                  
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  Your seed words and passphrase together open your wallet: do this only on your offline computer. Re-hide covers them; CLEAR, CLEAR ALL, auto-clear and END SESSION wipe them.
                  
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
    
                  
      Check a Coldcard seed mixSECRETNew Coldcard seeds mix your dice or coin flips with the device’s own random numbers. See that the mix is right.
      
                  Since firmware 1.5.1Q (Coldcard Q) and 5.6.1 (Mk4 and Mk5), a new Coldcard seed needs your own dice rolls, coin flips or key presses, and the device mixes them with its own random numbers (its TRNG words). From 1.5.2Q, 5.6.2 and Edge 6.6.1, View TRNG Words in that menu shows the device’s part as 24 words before you add yours. Type those 24 words and every roll or flip here: VOIDFORGE works out the words the Coldcard must show, by the formula in Coinkite’s published code. Key presses (Mash Keys) cannot be checked: they use the timing of the presses. A Coldcard dice-only seed (no device random numbers) is checked with Check your device’s dice, above.
                  
      
                  The TRNG words and your rolls together make the seed. Check a real seed only on your offline computer. Or practice first with a throwaway seed, then delete it on the Coldcard, because its words are no longer secret. Nothing here is saved, and CLEAR wipes it.
                  
      
      
                  
        
        
        
      
                  
      
      
                  0 / 50 rolls (at least 50 for the Coldcard)
                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      Was my seed made by a flawed device?NO KEYS NEEDEDSome devices and apps made weak seeds. Four questions; never type your words here.
      
                  A few devices and apps have had a flaw in the random numbers they used to make seeds. A seed made that way stays weak after an update: the fix only helps seeds made later. Answer the questions below. VOIDFORGE knows only the flaws its answer lists, so “no known flaw” is not a promise that a device is safe.
                  
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      Inspect a transaction (PSBT)READ ONLYSee where the money goes and the fee before signing.
      
                  Shows what a partly signed Bitcoin transaction (PSBT) from a wallet app would do: where the money comes from, where it goes, and the fee, so you can check it before signing on your hardware wallet. This only reads and displays. It cannot sign, never uses your seed words, and sends nothing. Paste the PSBT (base64 or hex) or choose the .psbt file. If you typed your words in the CHECK A BACKUP tab, outputs that carry this wallet’s key information are marked. It also checks any signatures it finds: whether two of them share a nonce (a repeated secret number that lets anyone work out the private key), whether a signature covers the whole transaction, and whether each signature is valid (it matches the transaction and the coin it spends). Each input says VALID, INVALID or NOT CHECKED (with why). A raw transaction does not carry the coins it spends, so its signatures can be checked only in Compare two transactions, next to the PSBT it came from.
                  
      
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      Compare two transactionsREAD ONLYDid the signer change anything? Is a fee bump a plain fee bump?
      
                  Paste the transaction you sent and the one that came back (from your signer or wallet). Or paste an original and its fee-bump replacement. This lists every difference in plain words, and checks every signature it can (for a raw transaction, with the coins named in the other one if that is a PSBT). It only reads and compares. It cannot sign and sends nothing anywhere.
                  
      
      
      
      
      
                  
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      What will spending cost later?NO KEYS NEEDEDHow the number of deposits and the address type change the fee to spend them.
      
                  Every deposit you receive becomes a separate coin, and spending pays a fee for each coin used. Many small deposits can cost more to spend than they are worth when fees are high. This works out the size of a payment that spends them all, and its fee at a few fee rates. It is arithmetic only: no network, no prices, sats only.
                  
      
                  
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      Verify a signed messageREAD ONLYCheck that the key of an address signed a message. This tool never signs.
      
                  Paste the address, the message exactly as it was signed, and the signature from the wallet that made it. Two formats are checked: the classic one (BIP137, from Bitcoin Core, Electrum, Sparrow, Trezor, Coldcard and others, for 1..., 3... and bc1q... addresses) and BIP322 “simple” signatures for single-key bc1q... and bc1p... addresses. A whole signed-message block (BEGIN BITCOIN SIGNED MESSAGE) can go in the message box. It only checks. It cannot sign and sends nothing. Every character of the message counts, including spaces and line breaks.
                  
      
      
      
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      Seed XOR: split or combineSECRETSplit one seed into 2 to 4 parts that are all needed, or combine parts, as Coldcard does.
      
                  Seed XOR (made by Coldcard) turns one 12, 18 or 24-word seed into 2, 3 or 4 parts. Each part is itself a normal-looking seed phrase that opens an empty wallet, so a thief who finds one part learns nothing. To get the seed back you need every part: lose one and the money is lost. That is the opposite of multisig, where some keys may be lost; if you want to survive a lost backup, use a 2-of-3 multisig instead. The passphrase, if any, is not split: it stays with the combined seed.
                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  Splits the words typed at the top of CHECK A BACKUP. As with the seed, the randomness comes from your dice: roll again (at least 50 times for 12 words, 75 for 18, 99 for 24) and type the results. Or choose the same parts a Coldcard makes for this seed: no rolls needed, but anyone who holds the seed can make those parts again (and can tell the parts came from it).
                  
        
                  
          
          
        
                  
        
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      SLIP39 shares (Shamir backup)SECRETCheck SLIP39 shares, combine them to see which wallet they open, or make new shares from dice.
      
                  A SLIP39 backup (a Shamir backup, made by Trezor and Keystone) is a set of shares of 20 or 33 words each, from a list of 1,024 words that is not the BIP39 list. A set number of them (for example 2 of 3) opens the wallet; fewer reveal nothing. Type each share on its own line. VOIDFORGE checks every share, and with enough of them shows the wallet’s master fingerprint and the first 10 receive and 10 change addresses, so you can compare them with your device. It can also make a new wallet as SLIP39 shares from your own dice rolls (choose “Make new SLIP39 shares from dice”). Do this only on your offline computer.
                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
        
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  Makes a new wallet, backed up as SLIP39 shares. As with a seed, the randomness comes from your dice only: roll at least 50 times for 20-word shares (128 bits) or 99 times for 33-word shares (256 bits) and type the results. Use new rolls, never the rolls of a seed you already use. The wallet’s secret is SHA-256 of the rolls, as in MAKE A SEED; the other random parts SLIP39 needs (the backup’s identifier and the share values) are worked out from the same rolls, so the same rolls and settings always give the same shares.
                  
        
                  This cannot turn seed words you already have into shares. A SLIP39 wallet is not the same wallet as BIP39 words, even from the same rolls: shares made from your words would open a different, empty wallet.
                  
        
                  
          
          
          
        
                  
        
        
                  
          
                  of the groups below, one per line: shares needed of shares in the group
                  
          
        
                  
        
        
        
                  The passphrase is optional. SLIP39 uses it to encrypt the wallet’s secret inside the shares; it is not a BIP39 passphrase (the “25th word”) and does not work like one. Every passphrase opens a wallet, with no error: a mistyped or forgotten one opens a different, empty wallet, so write it down apart from the shares. Only printable ASCII is allowed (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, space and the symbols on a US keyboard).
                  
        
                  
          
          
        
                  
        
                  Leave these as they are unless you know you need another value. New shares should be extendable, as SLIP39 says (more sets of shares can then be made later for the same wallet); turn it off only for a wallet app too old to read such shares. The iteration exponent sets how much work (PBKDF2 iterations) the passphrase takes to try; a higher one makes guessing a passphrase slower, and opening the wallet too.
                  
        
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      Codex32 shares (BIP93)SECRETCheck codex32 strings, combine shares to see which wallet they open, or make new shares from dice.
      
                  Codex32 (BIP93) writes a wallet’s master seed as one string of 48 characters (128 bits) or 74 (256 bits) that starts with MS1 and ends with a strong checksum. It can also be split into shares: a set number of them (2 to 9, for example 2 of 3) rebuilds the seed, and fewer reveal nothing. A codex32 seed is not the same wallet as BIP39 words: it is the BIP32 seed itself, with no word list and no passphrase, so the same randomness written as words opens a different wallet. Codex32 was made so that a person can check the checksum, and even make and combine shares, by hand with paper wheels called volvelles, with no computer at all. Coldcard reads and makes codex32 (firmware 5.6.3 on Mk4 and Mk5, 1.5.3Q on Q). Type each string on its own line (spaces are ignored). VOIDFORGE checks every string and says what is wrong with one, but it never corrects a string for you. With a secret (share index S) or enough shares it shows the wallet’s master fingerprint and the first 10 receive and 10 change addresses, so you can compare them with your device. It can also make a new wallet as codex32 shares from your own dice rolls (choose “Make new codex32 shares from dice”). Do this only on your offline computer.
                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  Makes a new wallet, backed up as codex32 shares (or as one codex32 secret that is not split). As with a seed, the randomness comes from your dice only: roll at least 50 times for a 128-bit seed (strings of 48 characters) or 99 times for 256 bits (74 characters) and type the results. Use new rolls, never the rolls of a seed you already use. The master seed is SHA-256 of the rolls, as in MAKE A SEED; the other random parts codex32 needs (the 4-character identifier and the first shares) are worked out from the same rolls, so the same rolls and settings always give the same strings. The shares are named A, C, D, E and so on, as BIP93 numbers them.
                  
        
                  This cannot turn seed words you already have into codex32. A codex32 wallet is not the same wallet as BIP39 words, even from the same rolls: codex32 made from your words would open a different, empty wallet.
                  
        
                  
          
          
          
        
                  
        
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      Child seed (BIP85)SECRETMake a separate new seed, key or password from this one.
      
                  Makes a brand new seed phrase from the parent words (and passphrase) typed in the CHECK A BACKUP tab, for a separate wallet, using the BIP85 standard. BIP85 can also make a Bitcoin Core HD seed (WIF), a master xprv, hex bytes, a password (Base64 or Base85) or dice rolls: choose one under “What to make”. The same parent, type, settings and index always give the same result. The child is as secret as the parent. It is shown here, with no copy or save; its print button prints it on one sheet, after asking, for a trusted offline printer only. Use the same safety steps as for a new seed, and keep the parent safe: if you lose the parent you lose every child.
                  
      
                  
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      Check your downloadPick the VOIDFORGE file you downloaded and compare its fingerprint with the published one.
      
                  Choose the voidforge.html file you downloaded. The page works out its SHA-256 hash and its content ID (CID) here on your computer, then compares them with the values from the release page (paste the hash, the CID, or a whole line of SHA256SUMS). The file is only read: it is not stored, changed or sent anywhere.
                  
      
                  Know the limit: a page cannot vouch for itself. A tampered copy could lie to you here, so for real money also run sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS with a tool that is not this page (RELEASING.md shows how). A copy saved with DOWNLOAD FOR USB is a re-saved page and will not match the release file.

Releases from v2.8.1 on are signed. The files are only read: nothing is stored or sent.
