Check the text on the phone before you open it. A QR code shows anyone what it holds, so this tool refuses anything that looks like a secret: seed words (also with typos, inside a link or after a label), SLIP39 shares, a private key, an xprv, SeedQR digits, dice rolls, a codex32 share, a passphrase after its label, or hex the size of a key. A transaction ID or a file’s hash is fine when you write txid or sha256 in front of it. It cannot know every secret: never paste one here.
                  
      
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
  
                  

  
                  
    
                  MULTISIG WALLETNEW
                  
    
                  Share control of your coins between several keys, so that no single lost or stolen key can empty the wallet.
                  
    
                  
      Set up a multisig walletGuided, one key at a time. Seeds are wiped from this page after each key.
      
                  
        
                  
          
                  What it is. A multisig wallet is built from N keys and spends only when M of them agree. With 2-of-3, losing one key loses nothing, and a thief with one key gets nothing.
                  
          
                  What it costs. More to back up, and setup takes longer. Every key is its own seed with its own paper backup, kept in a different place.
                  
          
                  How this works. You make one key at a time. After each, the seed is wiped from the page and only the public key is kept.
                  
        
                  
        
                  2-of-32 keys needed to spend, out of 3 total
                  
        
                  
          
          
        
                  
        
                  
          
                  
          
          
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  keys needed to spend (M)total keys (N)
                  
        
                  Popular: 
                  
        
                  
        
                  
          
          
          
        
                  
        
                  
          
                  Taproot multisig: new, and few wallets can sign it. The M-of-N rule sits in a hidden branch of a Taproot address (bc1p...), written tr(key, sortedmulti_a(M, keys)) (BIP386, BIP387). Until coins are spent, the address looks like any other Taproot address.
                  
          
                  Every spend shows the rule. A Taproot address can also be spent by one key alone (the key path). Here that key is made from BIP341’s point H, which nobody can sign with, so the key path is shut: every spend uses the multisig branch and shows the M-of-N rule and its keys. The key is an xpub on H whose chain code comes from the cosigner keys (the rule Nunchuk uses), so each address gets a different key and nothing random is needed.
                  
          
                  Key path m/48’/coin’/account’/3’. BIP48 defines only 1’ and 2’; there is no standard path for Taproot multisig. 3’ is the one Coldcard’s EDGE firmware uses. Nunchuk uses m/87’/... (BIP87) instead, so keys exported from Nunchuk do not fit here.
                  
          
                  Wallets that can sign it (checked in their source code and release notes): Bitcoin Core 24.0.1 or later (a descriptor wallet, through PSBT), and Coldcard Mk4 and Q with EDGE firmware (checked with 6.6.1X and 6.6.1QX; Coinkite’s preview firmware, which it recommends only for experimental use), which import the descriptor as a Miniscript wallet. Sparrow cannot use Taproot multisig yet. VOIDFORGE could not confirm other devices. Test with a small amount first.
                  
          
                  MuSig2 (BIP327), where the keys are combined into one key, is a different kind of Taproot multisig. VOIDFORGE does not make it.
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  TESTNET (practice coins only). These keys and addresses are not for real money.
                  
        
                  
        
                  
          
                  Paste the public key of another signer: a Zpub/xpub, or the whole [fingerprint/48h/...]xpub... line from their device. Never paste a private key or seed words here.

                  All keys were made on this one device. That is convenient, but it puts every key in one place for a while: anyone who could read this device’s memory during setup could get all of them. For real protection, make each key on a different device (or at least after a restart), store each backup in a different place, and use the paste option above to combine only the public keys.

                      Encrypted descriptor backup (BIP138)
                      

                      Without the descriptor, the seeds alone cannot find this wallet’s coins, so keep extra copies of it. This saves it encrypted as a .bip138 file, the format Liana writes: store copies anywhere, even online. It opens only with one of the wallet’s keys (its words, or just its xpub), and on its own it shows nothing about the wallet. The encryption needs a number used only once (a nonce), and VOIDFORGE never makes randomness itself: roll a die at least 50 times and type the results.

                      The descriptor contains only public keys. It lets a wallet app watch the balance and make receiving addresses; it cannot spend. To spend you need M of the seeds, so keep every seed backup safe, and keep a copy of this descriptor (the recovery sheet) with them: without it, the seeds alone are not enough to find the funds.

VOIDFORGE lists every public key in them and warns when a key appears twice, when two keys of one multisig come from the same seed, or when the same fingerprint and path give different keys. Private keys are refused.
                      
      
      
                      
      
                      
    
                      
    
                      
      Find a typo in a descriptorPUBLIC KEYS ONLYA descriptor that will not import, or a checksum that does not match: which character is wrong.
      
                      Paste the descriptor exactly as it was written down or copied, with its checksum (the 8 characters after #). One wrong character always changes the checksum, so VOIDFORGE tries every single change (a character replaced, two neighbors swapped, one left out or added) and shows the one that makes the descriptor match its checksum again, with every key valid. It only reads public keys; it cannot spend.

                      Inheritance and recovery wallets (Liana, Nunchuk’s timelocked wallets, Bitcoin Core) are described by a descriptor with conditions such as older(52560). Paste it here: VOIDFORGE lists every way the coins can be spent, which keys must sign, and how long each one has to wait. With the seed words typed in CHECK A BACKUP, it also says which key those words are. Type the current block height (any block explorer, or your wallet app, shows it) to turn a fixed block into a rough date. It only reads public keys; it cannot spend.

                      ⚠ BEFORE YOU MAKE REAL KEYS
                      

                      Three ways a computer can quietly keep your secrets, and the simple fix for each.
                      

                      1
                      Your computer may keep a copy of your keys. It can write memory to the hard drive (swap files, hibernation) without asking, and the browser cannot stop it.What to do: for real money, use an offline computer with an encrypted drive, and turn hibernation off.
                      

                      2
                      Copying can leak. Clipboard history can keep what you copy or paste, and may sync it to your other devices.What to do: write seeds on paper; avoid copy and paste for anything secret, and turn clipboard history off.
                      

                      3
                      Keys can stay in memory after you finish. Wiping the page is a precaution, not a guarantee.What to do: when you are done, close the browser and restart the computer.
                      

  
                      
    
                      IS ANYTHING WATCHING THIS PAGE?
                      
    
                      Browser extensions (password managers, writing assistants, translators, wallet extensions) and other software can read a page and everything typed into it, including seed words. This looks for the signs they leave on this page: scripts, frames and elements it never makes, attributes it never sets, translation, objects that wallet extensions add, a frame around the page, and automation. It checks by itself as the page runs and shows a warning at the top when it finds one. It can only find signs, so it never says the page is safe.
                      
    
                      
    
                      
    
                      
  
                      

  
                      
    
                      ABOUT & HELP
                      
    
                      VOIDFORGE is an educational tool. It is open source, works fully offline and is meant to be read, but it has not been independently audited. Use it to learn and to make keys you understand, practice first, and start real money with a small amount.
                      
    
                      
      How to use
      
                        
        
                      1. Copy this single file to a USB stick and open it on an air-gapped computer.
                        2. 
        
                      2. Press SELF-TEST and confirm it says all tests passed.
                        3. 
        
                      3. Choose Dice or Coin (or Word draw if you drew physical word tiles), enter your physical rolls or flips, and press FORGE SEED. For coins, decide which side is 1 and which is 0 (heads = 1, tails = 0 is the usual choice), use it for every flip, and record the exact 1/0 string with your backup. You can type, paste, or tap the buttons above the box.
                        4. 
        
                      4. Compare the words and the master fingerprint with a second independent offline tool before trusting real funds.
                        5. 
        
                      5. To check a backup later, type the words into VERIFY, add the passphrase if you used one, and paste the fingerprint or first address you wrote down into the last box. VERIFY tells you whether it matches without a passphrase, with it, or neither.
                        6. 
      
                      
    
                      
    
                      
      Hardware wallet: SeedSignerRECOMMENDED
      
                      For real funds, VOIDFORGE recommends SeedSigner as the signing device. It is open source (MIT license); it stores no seed (seeds live only in its memory and are wiped when it is switched off); and it talks to your wallet app only through QR codes. It makes seeds from 50 or 99 dice rolls and backs them up as SeedQR, which VOIDFORGE can make and check the same way. These points come from its own source code (release 0.8.7). A recommendation is not a guarantee: verify the SeedSigner software you install as its project explains, and keep using VOIDFORGE to cross-check its words, fingerprint and addresses. To try its screens and buttons first, use the Practice signer in CHECK A BACKUP (practice only, never for real coins).

      Browser safety checklistEight quick habits that keep your seed on the page and nowhere else.
      
                      This page works offline, but the browser and computer around it can still keep copies of what you see. None of these steps is hard, and each one closes a real gap.
                      
      
                        
        
                      1. Go offline first. Turn off Wi-Fi and unplug the network cable before you open the page. The “WARNING: this computer looks ONLINE” banner is only a hint, so do not rely on it.
                        2. 
        
                      2. For real funds, open the file from a USB stick or a local folder on an offline computer, never from a website. Check the file’s SHA256 first (see the README). The online copy on the project page is for practice only. Its address is random21m.github.io/VOIDFORGE, the only link on this page; it opens in a new tab, and your browser contacts that site only if you click it.
                        3. 
        
                      3. Use a fresh browser window with extensions turned off. A private window is not enough: extensions can still read every page.
                        4. 
        
                      4. Turn off page translation, read-aloud and screen sharing. Translation tools may send the page text, including your words, to a server.
                        5. 
        
                      5. Mind the clipboard. Copying seed words or a SeedQR can leave them in clipboard history, and some systems sync that history. Clear it afterwards, or write by hand instead of copying.
                        6. 
        
                      6. Printing and “save as PDF” make files. Delete them and check the printer queue afterwards. A printer that is not on a network is best.
                        7. 
        
                      7. Check the Downloads folder and any auto-saved files when you are done, and delete anything you made.
                        8. 
        
                      8. Finish by closing the page, then restart the browser or, better, the computer. That clears what the page left in memory.
                        9. 
      
                      
      
                      A browser is not a hardware wallet. This checklist lowers the risk; it does not remove it, which is why we also ask you to test with a small amount first.
                      
    
                      
    
                      
      Privacy: what this page does with your dataWhat it keeps, what it never sends, and the only ways anything leaves.
      
                        
        
                      • Nothing is sent anywhere. The page has no code that talks to the internet, and a rule built into the file (a Content-Security-Policy) tells the browser to block all network access as a second line of defense. You can read the file to check; there is no server, no account and no tracking.
                        • 
        
                      • Only two things are remembered between visits: your light or dark choice and your text size, in your browser’s local storage. Your rolls, flips, words, passphrase and fingerprint are never stored. Close the page and they are gone from the page.
                        • 
        
                      • One note for this tab only: while the computer is offline, closing the start notice puts a single “1” in this tab’s session storage, so the notice does not come back every time you reload. It lasts only as long as the tab, and END SESSION (MENU) deletes it straight away. Nothing else goes there, and nothing at all while the computer is online.
                        • 
        
                      • Your secrets live only in the page’s memory while it is open. The WIPE button and closing the tab clear them from the page, but not from anything your computer copied in the meantime (see the safety checklist above).
                        • 
        
                      • Things leave the page only when you press a button for them: COPY (to your clipboard), PRINT, and DOWNLOAD. Each one makes a copy outside the page, so each is your call.
                        • 
        
                      • Secret and public are labeled. Words, the passphrase and SeedQR are secret. The fingerprint, addresses, watch-only export and multisig descriptor are public data, safe to show a second computer, though they let others see your balance.
                        • 
        
                      • The practice backup uses a public test seed, not a real seed. It is one of the published BIP39 test vectors, used only to practice writing words down. The page makes no random numbers of its own.
                        • 
      
                      
    
                      
    
                      
      How multisig works, and what it costsSeveral keys, any M of them can spend. Read this before you set one up.
      
                      A multisig wallet is built from N separate seeds and spends only when M of them agree. With 2-of-3 you can lose one seed, or have one stolen, and still be safe. It is the standard way to remove the “one piece of paper” risk.
                      
      
                        
        
                      • Back up the descriptor too. The seeds alone are not enough: to find the money you also need the list of all the public keys (the descriptor, or the printed recovery sheet). It contains no secrets, so keep copies in several places.
                        • 
        
                      • Keep every seed in a different place, and make each one on a different day or device if you can.
                        • 
        
                      • Never reuse a seed as two of the keys, or the same seed in two different multisig wallets of the same account.
                        • 
        
                      • Test with a small amount first, and practice recovering with M of the seeds before you trust it with real savings.
                        • 
        
                      • Spending needs a wallet app (Sparrow, Nunchuk, Bitcoin Core) plus signers. VOIDFORGE only sets the wallet up; its tools never sign. Only the practice signer signs. It runs inside this page, so it is as safe as the page itself: use it on an offline computer.
                        • 
      
                      
    
                      
    
                      
      Method
      
                      SHA256(input string) → first 16 bytes (12 words) or 32 bytes (24 words) → BIP39 mnemonic + checksum
                      
      
                      
        
                      WordsDice rolls (1–6)Coin flips (1/0)
                      
        
                      1250128
                      
        
                      2499256
                      
      
                      
      
                      The roll or flip string is hashed as plain text. Dice are digits 1–6; coin flips are the characters 1 and 0 (choose which side counts as 1 and keep the exact string). This is the same method SeedSigner uses for its 12/24-word dice seeds (and in its coin-flip code), and VOIDFORGE reproduces SeedSigner’s published dice examples. Coldcard uses the same dice method (SHA-256 of the roll digits as plain text; 24 words, or the first half of the hash for 12), and VOIDFORGE reproduces the worked example in Coldcard’s documentation: the rolls 123456 give mirror reject rookie … garment (24 words). That example is too short to be safe; it only proves the method matches. Only 12- and 24-word seeds are generated, so every seed can be reproduced by SeedSigner-style tools. The VERIFY box still accepts 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24-word phrases from other tools.
                      
    
                      
    
                      
      Master fingerprint & first ten addresses
      
                      PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512(mnemonic, "mnemonic"+passphrase, 2048) → seed
                      
         HMAC-SHA512("Bitcoin seed", seed) → master private key
                      
         secp256k1 pubkey → RIPEMD160(SHA256(pubkey)) → first 4 bytes
                      
      
                      Fingerprint picture. Next to the master fingerprint is a small colored picture (a LifeHash, version 2, made from SHA-256 of the fingerprint). Sparrow Wallet shows the same picture for the same fingerprint, so a matching picture is a quick visual sign that you are looking at the same wallet. It is only a convenience: the 8-character fingerprint and the addresses are the real checks, and the picture does not depend on your keys beyond the fingerprint.
                      
      
                      Watch-only export. After FORGE, the box “Watch-only wallet” shows the public key of the account m/84’/0’/0’ as a zpub (Electrum, Blue Wallet, Sparrow) and as output descriptors wpkh([fingerprint/84h/0h/0h]xpub…/0/*) for receiving and /1/* for change, with the descriptor checksum (Sparrow, Nunchuk, Bitcoin Core). The Network menu switches to testnet (test coins only; keys start with tpub, upub or vpub). The two Multisig cosigner choices give the BIP48 key (Zpub or Ypub) plus its origin, to add as one cosigner in a multisig wallet. The Address type menu switches it to Taproot (tr, BIP86), Nested SegWit (sh(wpkh), BIP49, ypub) or Legacy (pkh, BIP44), and the Account box changes the account number (almost always 0). It holds no private keys and cannot spend, but whoever has it can see every address and balance of that wallet, so give it only to your own wallet app. It is specific to the passphrase you entered. The SHOW QR buttons draw the same data as a QR code on screen so another device can scan it (many apps accept a scanned zpub or descriptor; if yours does not, use COPY). After importing, check that the app’s first receive address equals the First receive address shown here.
                      
      
                      First ten receive and ten change addresses. Also shown are the first 10 receive and the first 10 change Bitcoin mainnet addresses of a standard native SegWit (BIP84) wallet: BIP32 child keys along m/84’/0’/0’/0/0 to 0/9 (receive) and m/84’/0’/0’/1/0 to 1/9 (change), each then RIPEMD160(SHA256(pubkey)) encoded as a bc1q… bech32 address; the first one is also shown right under the fingerprint. Use them to cross-check against a wallet that imports the same words (a watch-only wallet is enough): the fingerprint alone is a weak check, matching addresses are a strong one, and comparing all twenty is stronger than comparing one. They are only correct for wallets that use the BIP84 path; other wallet types (legacy, nested SegWit) show different addresses, and the Taproot list (BIP86) is shown separately. They include the passphrase if you entered one; VERIFY shows them without a passphrase and, if you type one into its own passphrase box, with it too.
                      
      
                      RIPEMD-160 and secp256k1 are implemented in this file (no libraries). The curve code is not constant-time, which is fine offline but another reason never to run this on a networked or shared computer. The fingerprint includes the optional BIP39 passphrase; VERIFY shows it without a passphrase and, if you type one into its own passphrase box, with it too.
                      
    
                      
    
                      
      What SELF-TEST checks
      
                      It runs automatically every time the page loads; if any test fails, seed generation is disabled and a red banner appears. Press SELF-TEST to see the full list. It checks: the BIP39 wordlist hash; official BIP39 entropy vectors (12 to 24 words); SeedSigner’s published 50- and 99-roll dice examples and 50-roll fingerprint; coin-flip vectors from an independent reference implementation of SeedSigner’s method; the abandon…about fingerprints (with and without the TREZOR passphrase); BIP32 test vector 1; the first receive address (the published BIP84 vector, a second vector from two independent libraries, and the BIP173 bech32 example); the watch-only zpub (published BIP84 vector and an independent-library vector), the descriptor checksum, a QR code matrix checked against an independent QR library, and the fingerprint picture checked against independent LifeHash code and Sparrow Wallet; passphrase normalization; RIPEMD-160 vectors; the phrase checker; and, added since, Keystone dice rules, the dice passphrase, coin-flip and word-draw helpers, Electrum seeds, every address type and its account keys on mainnet and testnet, Taproot (BIP86 and the BIP350 example), multisig cosigner keys and addresses (BIP48), Silent Payment addresses (BIP352), private key versions (SLIP132), BIP85 child seeds, keys and passwords (published vectors), SeedQR and CompactSeedQR, signed messages (BIP137 and BIP322 vectors), the transaction inspector on a known PSBT, Reforge, Ed25519 signatures (RFC 8032 vectors) and the release key’s fingerprint, a playing-card seed (as Ian Coleman’s BIP39 tool makes it, hashed and as raw entropy) and 15, 18 and 21-word seeds, SLIP39 shares (an official test vector, and shares made from fixed dice rolls), old Electrum seeds (the old word list’s hash and Electrum’s own test wallets), Reforge’s damaged-word patterns, public example phrases, look-alike letters and rolls typed twice, punch plate numbers, signature checks (legacy, SegWit and Taproot signature hashes, and one signature checked valid and, with 1 sat less, invalid), Coinkite’s Coldcard seed mix examples, encrypted descriptor backups (the official BIP138 vectors, and a miniscript and a Taproot-tree address from embit), and codex32 strings (the BIP93 test vectors, and shares made from fixed dice rolls). If any test fails, do not use that copy for real funds.
                      
      
                      What the self-test cannot catch: it only runs known answers through this same file, so it can miss a bug on inputs it does not cover, and a tampered file could simply fake a pass. It does not replace checking the file’s SHA256 against the release, and it does not replace comparing your words and fingerprint in a second independent tool. The network tag at the top reads the browser’s online flag only; it cannot prove the machine is air-gapped.
                      
    
                      
    
                      
      Security notes
      
                        
        
                      • Only use this offline, on a computer. Never type a real seed into a phone, website or online tool; phones and file previews often will not run this page at all.
                        • 
        
                      • The randomness meter checks face counts, long runs, repeating or stepping patterns and periodic repeats. It is advisory only: it catches lazy input, not subtle bias, and cannot prove your dice or coin are good. If it flags a pattern, FORGE SEED asks before continuing.
                        • 
        
                      • A Content-Security-Policy built into this file tells the browser to block all network access, as a second line of defense. It does not replace using an offline computer.
                        • 
        
                      • This page contains no links, and switching between dice and coin clears the entered rolls (after asking).
                        • 
        
                      • The red “WARNING: this computer looks ONLINE” banner is a hint from the browser, not proof. A machine can be connected without the browser knowing, so physically disconnect it.
                        • 
        
                      • Text boxes turn off spellcheck, autofill and autocorrect so the browser doesn’t keep what you type. The passphrase is masked, and is never shown with, copied with, printed with or saved with the words.
                        • 
        
                      • There is deliberately no "copy seed" button. SEND TO CHECK moves the words to the VERIFY box without the clipboard, but that only re-runs the same code. For a real check, write the words down by hand and type them into a second tool. The clipboard is where seeds most often leak. PRINT SEED and DOWNLOAD ask for confirmation because the print spooler and your disk can retain the seed.
                        • 
        
                      • DOWNLOAD FOR USB saves a clean copy of this page and never includes a generated seed. It is re-serialized by the browser, so its file hash will not match the original; to verify a hash, copy the original file instead. DOWNLOAD (seed) writes your seed and rolls to a plain-text file, so only use it on a trusted offline machine.
                        • 
        
                      • VOIDFORGE has not been independently audited. This software is provided “as is”, without warranty of any kind (MIT license), and the author is not liable for any loss. You alone are responsible for your funds, your backups and how you use it. If you lose the words or the passphrase, nobody can recover the funds. Before trusting it, check the release hash, use an offline computer, restore the wallet from your written backup in a second tool, and move a small amount first. It is not financial, legal or security advice.

HOLD UP TO THE DEVICE shows it to the device’s camera, and the device reviews it exactly as a real SeedSigner does (what comes in, each payment with its address and amount, change checked by derivation path or wallet descriptor, the fee, SeedSigner’s own warnings) and signs with the loaded seed. The signed PSBT comes back as the device’s animated QR, as base64 to copy and as a .psbt file, byte for byte what SeedSigner makes, and this page checks every signature with its own code.                       • 2.14.0 — The Damascus method, and lessons on the practice signer. MAKE A SEED has a new Damascus tab: a 12- or 24-word seed made by hand from dice and playing cards, folded together and checked as you go. The dice fill the Hammer sheet, the cards fill the Anvil sheet, and folding them (same bits give 0, different bits give 1) gives the Forge sheet, whose rows you look up in a printed word table. If either the dice or the shuffle is good, the seed is random. Hallmarks (an odd-ones check on every row and column) catch copying mistakes, not cheating, and they reveal part of the seed (22 bits for 12 words, 34 for 24), so keep them only next to the words. The last word needs a computer: the tab says how to get it from a SeedSigner (or the practice signer) and from VOIDFORGE, and both must agree. Its 7 bits (3 for 24 words) come from the Forge sheet; they are not new coin flips. On screen it goes in five steps (Hammer, Anvil, Forge, Words, Last word) with a progress bar: tap the dice on the Dice tab’s faces (two taps a pair) and the cards on the Cards & hex tab’s card picker, and each row, deck and word is checked as you finish it, with a mistake shown where it is. The last step shows the last word, fingerprint and first address, or works the last word out from the Forge sheet alone (CALCULATE LAST WORD, as SeedSigner’s Calc 12th/24th word does). The tab has a quick guide and questions, three public worked examples, a practice run (a practice sheet made from a published rule, never from the page’s random numbers, so anyone can make the same one), CHECK MY SHEETS (it works out every grid, hallmark and word and points to the row and column of a mistake), an assay (a second person checks one sheet only and sees that sheet’s hallmarks and its own Seed XOR phrase, never the seed), and a printable kit: PRINT DAMASCUS KIT, the three sheets, the word table, a backup card and a trial checklist, on Letter or A4. CHECK A BACKUP has Recheck a Damascus backup: type the words and the hallmarks written next to them. It takes about 30 minutes once you know the steps, and was field-tested on a real SeedSigner and in Sparrow on 10 November 2026. The method is credited on the tab and in ABOUT & HELP: “The Damascus method, created by Random, 10 November 2026”, with its origin record (tag damascus-origin-2026-11-10, Bitcoin block 975,337). The self-test now has 141 checks, one of them the first worked example. The practice signer has six lessons beside the device: make a seed from dice, load a seed and export the xpub, check a receive address, sign a transaction, set up and check a 2-of-3 multisig, and sign a message. Each step says what to press and what you should see, and moves on by itself when the device shows the right screen. Nothing is drawn on the device’s screen. A practice transaction button makes a PSBT that spends made-up coins, holds it up to the device’s camera, and after you sign it checks every signature on the page. Its coins do not exist, so it can never be broadcast. The lessons use public test seeds only (such as abandon ... about): never put coins on them. A card under the header and MENU > PRACTICE SIGNER open it. CLEAR ALL, auto-clear, END SESSION and closing the box wipe the lessons and the practice transaction. Below the device, FORGE SEED takes a seed loaded on the practice signer into MAKE A SEED’s usual result, marked PRACTICE (the device’s fingerprint next to this page’s is a consistency check only, not an independent one), and a practice Damascus seed goes onto the practice signer with LOAD INTO THE PRACTICE SIGNER, which takes practice seeds only (its SeedQR is held up to the device’s camera). New dictionary entries: Damascus method, Hammer sheet, Anvil sheet, Forge sheet, Hallmark, Skew hallmark, Assay, Bias box, Binary word table, Practice sheet and Practice transaction.

(1) Check your device’s dice (EXTRA TOOLS): type throwaway test rolls and see the words a SeedSigner, Coldcard or Keystone must show for them, by each device’s own dice rules, and its first receive address. If the device shows other words although the rolls and its dice rules are the same, its dice seeds cannot be trusted. BitBox02 takes no dice, so you restore the test words on it and compare the address. PRINT TEST CARD prints public test rolls with the words each device must make. Test rolls and their words are not secret: reset the device before making your real wallet. (2) Make a passphrase from dice (Passphrase and note): new rolls, never the seed’s own, become a passphrase of 6 or 8 BIP39 words (66 or 88 bits), hashed with SHA-256 as for the seed, and the rolls make it again, so they are kept with it, never with the seed rolls; USE AS PASSPHRASE puts it in both passphrase boxes. (3) Two wallets side by side (Open this wallet): with a passphrase, the wallet without it and the wallet with it, each with its fingerprint and first address, and a plain word on decoy wallets. (4) Roll together (Make a seed): how two people, or two dice, make one seed, and why each die should roll the full count. New dictionary entries: Device dice check, Dice passphrase and Roll together. Seed words, fingerprints, addresses, keys and descriptors are unchanged.

(1) Animated QR for a multisig wallet (Multisig wallet): no one format reaches every device, so pick yours: UR crypto-output for Sparrow, SeedSigner and Nunchuk; BBQr for Coldcard Q; or UR bytes carrying the Coldcard-style setup file for Keystone and Passport. Three frame sizes, and PAUSE. Public keys only. (2) The Inspect a transaction (PSBT) also reads the text of an animated QR code pasted as parts (UR crypto-psbt or BBQr), one part per line. (3) Open this wallet takes a custom account path (such as m/0' for some older apps), and Or open a private key, read only opens an xprv, yprv or zprv (or tprv, uprv, vprv), a WIF key or a Casascius mini key to show which addresses it controls. It never signs; the key is wiped by CLEAR ALL, auto-clear and END SESSION, and in practice mode only test-network keys open. (4) Check an address before you pay (CHECK A BACKUP, under Explain an address): compares the address you are about to pay with the one you were given, character by character, and warns when only the start and the end match, as in address poisoning and clipboard-swap scams. (5) What will spending cost later? (EXTRA TOOLS): the size and the fee of spending many small deposits, by address type. (6) Fixes: CLEAR ALL now also wipes the Reforge boxes, the words or passphrase Reforge found, and the practice words box. In practice mode COPY ADDRESS copies the test-network address, and VERIFY checks a recorded first address on its own network (a bc1q address against the real one, a tb1q address against the test-network one). A seed file saved from Word draw says the words were drawn by hand and gives the coin flips, not what was in the rolls box. CHECK ADDRESS and Try accounts 0 to 20 say when an address is a multisig script address (P2WSH) instead of searching for it.                       • 1.29.0 — More from BIP85: keys, passwords and dice. The Child seed (BIP85) card in EXTRA TOOLS has a new “What to make” choice. Besides seed words it now makes every other BIP85 output a wallet or password manager can use: a Bitcoin Core HD seed (WIF), a master xprv (shown with its master fingerprint), hex bytes (16 to 64), a password in Base64 (20 to 86 characters) or Base85 (10 to 80), and dice rolls for any die from 2 to 2,147,483,647 sides (up to 1,000 rolls, numbered from 0 as BIP85 says). All are recreated from the parent words, passphrase, type, settings and index, and all are secret like the parent. Dice need SHAKE256, which the page now has; it is checked in the self-test against the published BIP85 vector and in the tests against Node’s own SHAKE256. Every new output matches the published BIP85 test vectors and an independent implementation. Seed words, fingerprints, addresses, keys and descriptors are unchanged from v1.28.0. The project owner’s logo (a bloodhound in a worn cap) now shows in the top-right corner as a small picture built into the file (not a link, nothing loaded from the network); it is left off printouts. The page now tells browsers not to translate it, because a translated seed word is a wrong seed word; if your browser offers to translate anyway, say no. The passphrase help also notes that some hardware wallets limit passphrase length or characters, so test a small amount first.

                      • 1.28.0 — Reforge: recover a seed or find a passphrase. A new Reforge tool in EXTRA TOOLS replaces Find the last word. In Missing or wrong words you type your words with ? for any you lack; it fills in one or two unknown words, finds one wrong word or two swapped words, or puts back a word missing from an unknown place, and checks every candidate against your wallet’s master fingerprint, an address (receive addresses 0 to 9 of account 0) or its account xpub/ypub/zpub, with your passphrase if you use one. In Passphrase it tries your guesses alone and joined in twos and threes, in four letter cases, and optionally with one typo. It reports only what matched, says how likely a fingerprint match is to be a coincidence, says plainly when nothing matched and what it searched, refuses an address with a typo before starting, and STOP ends a long search. Typing 11 words and ? lists the possible last words, as Find the last word did, and 4-letter word forms are read. Every search plan is checked in the test suite against independent libraries (@scure/bip39, @scure/bip32, @scure/btc-signer). Also: a typed word that happens to be a JavaScript property name (such as “constructor”) is now reported as an unknown word in CHECK A BACKUP instead of as a failed checksum. The dice logo now shows as the page icon in a tab or bookmark (built into the file, no network), and the About page now says the online copy on the project page is for practice only and links to it. Closing the opening notice no longer pops up the on-screen keyboard on a phone or tablet. This is the only link on the page; it opens in a new tab and does nothing unless you click it. Words, fingerprints, addresses, keys and descriptors are unchanged from v1.27.3.

                      VOIDFORGE v2.17.0
                      
    
                      
    
                      SHA-256 of your rolls → BIP39Same method as SeedSigner and Coldcardgithub.com/Random21m/VOIDFORGE
                      
  
                      

                      

                      

                      


                      

                      CAMERA ON
                      

                      

                      Before you make real keys
                      

                      VOIDFORGE is an educational tool. It works fully offline and never stores your rolls, words or keys, and its code is open to read, but it has not been independently audited. Your computer, though, can keep secrets. Three things worth knowing first:
                      

                      1
                      Your computer may keep a copy of your keys. It can write memory to the hard drive (swap files, hibernation) without asking, and the browser cannot stop it.What to do: for real money, use an offline computer with an encrypted drive, and turn hibernation off.
                      

                      2
                      Copying can leak. Clipboard history can keep what you copy or paste, and may sync it to your other devices.What to do: write seeds on paper; avoid copy and paste for anything secret, and turn clipboard history off.
                      

                      3
                      Keys can stay in memory after you finish. Wiping the page is a precaution, not a guarantee.What to do: when you are done, close the browser and restart the computer.
                      

                      


                      Practicing with a test seed? Nothing here applies. For real money, start with a small amount. Offline, this shows once in each browser tab; online, every time the page opens. END SESSION in the MENU wipes the page and shows it again.
